title: Signs and symbols (CCC 1145–1152)
hook: water, oil, bread, wine, light: creation speaks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole Christ celebrates: heaven and earth, priest and people, all at one liturgy. Your line was all of us. Did a small moment turn out to be more crowded than it looked? Day one thousand eighty-nine.

Could a faith get by on ideas alone, with nothing to touch? The Catholic Church doesn't try to. At its most solemn moments, it reaches for things any household keeps. Water poured over a baby's head. Oil traced on a forehead. Bread and wine on an altar. A candle burning beside a coffin. Holiness, carried by plain stuff. A visitor might find that odd. The Catechism doesn't, and its explanation begins where this path went earlier, with body and soul as one person. Today's word is what the Church calls these things.
screen: `IDEAS ALONE?` → `WATER, OIL, BREAD, A FLAME.` → `IT BEGINS WITH THE BODY.`

segments.voice: First, people need signs. The Catechism says it simply: human beings are body and spirit together, so they take in and express spiritual things through physical ones. A hug says more than a memo. A ring says something a contract can't. The liturgy works the same way. Second, creation already speaks. The Catechism says God talks to people through the visible world: light and darkness, wind and fire, water and earth, the tree and its fruit. A psalm says it in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands." So when the Church uses water or light, it isn't inventing a code. It's picking up a language creation was already speaking. Third, God's covenant gave these things a history. The Catechism points to the signs of Israel's covenant with God: anointing kings and priests, laying on hands, sacrifice, and above all the Passover. Bread and wine and oil already carried memories long before the Church used them. Fourth, Jesus used them too. In John's Gospel he meets a man born blind. He spits on the ground, makes a little mud, spreads it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. The man comes back seeing. Earth and spit and water, of all things. The Catechism says he gave ordinary things a new meaning, and that since Pentecost, the Holy Spirit works through the Church's signs, the sacraments, to make people holy. So the bread on your counter and the bread on the altar are not the same in Catholic belief. But the one on your counter is not nothing either. In the Catechism's picture, it's part of the same language.
screen: `BODY AND SPIRIT NEED SIGNS.` · `THE HEAVENS SHEW FORTH.` · `SIGNS OF THE COVENANT.` · `MUD ON A BLIND MAN'S EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: handle bread with reverence. If there's bread nearby, take a piece in your hands. If not, a glass of water, or anything you'll eat or drink today. Settle, and breathe. Hold it, and look at it properly, the way you'd look at a gift. Think about where it came from: the field, the rain, the hands that made it and moved it. Feel its weight. If you pray, you can give thanks before you eat it. If you don't, simply let yourself be grateful for it. Then eat or drink slowly, as if it meant something. The bell holds the time.
Signs and symbols. Water, oil, bread, wine and light, taken from creation, carried by Israel's covenant, used by Jesus, and in the sacraments, Catholics believe, used by the Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: creation speaks. Today, pick one ordinary thing you touch, water, bread, light through a window, and let it say something before you use it. Day one thousand eighty-nine.

howItsDone: In the sacraments Catholics use water in baptism, oil in confirmation and anointing, bread and wine at Mass, and candles at baptisms, funerals and the Easter Vigil.

fork.setup: in John's Gospel, Jesus meets a man born blind. how does he heal him?

fork.reveal: he spits on the ground, makes clay, spreads it on the man's eyes, and sends him to wash. earth and water, used for healing.

trapdoor: what you thought: symbols are decorations on the real thing.
what it means: Catholics believe God speaks through creation, and in the sacraments uses water, oil, bread, wine and light.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism traces each sign through creation, Israel's covenant and Christ's own actions, like the mud in John 9.

sources.quoted: The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands.

notes: CCC paraphrased (1146 humans as body and spirit express and perceive spiritual realities through physical signs; 1147 God speaks through visible creation: light and darkness, wind and fire, water and earth, tree and fruit; 1150 covenant signs: circumcision, anointing and consecration of kings and priests, laying on of hands, sacrifices, above all the Passover; 1151 Christ's use of signs, including material signs; 1152 since Pentecost the Spirit sanctifies through sacramental signs). Circumcision is not named in the script. Confirm.
John 9 is cited by the CCC (1151, 'clay of spittle' among Christ's signs); confirm.
'The bread on your counter and the bread on the altar are not the same in Catholic belief' refers to the Eucharist, taught later in Part Two; kept brief.

Editor pass: hook rewritten (it was a list of household objects, the same device and many of the same objects as day 1079's hook) to open on a question and call back to day 1072's body and soul; cut the narrator's 'Jesus didn't need the mud', which the text does not say, and the matching 'you could heal him with a word' fork setup; 'part of the same language' attributed to the Catechism's picture.
